instruction: From an access log, find the ten client IPs that made the most requests.
response: awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10
context: The count-and-rank idiom: awk projects the field, sort groups equal values adjacently so uniq -c can count them, and the second sort -rn ranks by that count descending. uniq only collapses adjacent lines, which is why the first sort is mandatory.

instruction: Show how many times each HTTP status code appears in an access log.
context: awk: $9 is the status field in the combined log format. Counting distinct values of one column is the same sort/uniq -c/sort -rn shape regardless of which field is projected.

instruction: Total the bytes transferred across every request in an access log.
context: awk: an accumulator variable needs no declaration and starts at zero. The END block runs once after the last record, which is where the running total gets printed.

instruction: Compute the average response time from the last column of a timing log.
response: awk '{sum += $NF; n++} END {if (n) print sum / n}' timings.log
context: awk: $NF is the last field, so the expression survives varying column counts. Guarding the division with if (n) avoids a divide-by-zero on empty input.

instruction: Sum the bytes sent per client IP and print the biggest consumers first.
response: awk '{bytes[$1] += $10} END {for (ip in bytes) print bytes[ip], ip}' access.log | sort -rn | head -20
context: awk: associative arrays index by any string, so bytes[$1] accumulates per IP in a single pass. The END loop emits the map, and sorting is left to sort because awk's for-in order is unspecified.

instruction: List every user account that has a real login shell from /etc/passwd.
context: awk: -F sets the input field separator, so -F: splits the colon-delimited passwd format. The !~ operator negates a regex match, and the $ anchors it to the end of the field.

instruction: Show filesystems that are more than eighty percent full.
context: df: -P forces the portable single-line format so a long device name cannot wrap and shift the columns. awk's int() truncates the percent sign off $5, and NR > 1 skips the header.

instruction: Search only the recently modified source files for a symbol.
context: The NUL-safe hand-off: -print0 emits names separated by NUL, the only byte illegal in a filename, and xargs -0 consumes that framing. -r skips the grep entirely when nothing matched.

instruction: Checksum every file in a release directory in parallel and save the manifest.
response: find release -type f -print0 | xargs -0 -r -P 8 -n 32 sha256sum > SHA256SUMS
context: xargs: -P 8 runs eight workers and -n 32 hands each one thirty-two paths, which amortizes process startup. Output interleaving is safe here because each sha256sum line is written atomically when short.

instruction: Run a build while both watching the output and saving it to a log file.
context: tee duplicates its input to a file and to stdout. The 2>&1 must precede the pipe so stderr is redirected into stdout before the pipeline is set up; placing it after tee would capture only tee's own errors.

instruction: Append monitoring output to an existing log without truncating it.
context: tee: -a appends rather than truncating, matching >> instead of >. Without -a the existing log is emptied the moment the pipeline starts, before any new output arrives.

instruction: List the distinct login shells configured on this machine.
context: cut projects a single field and sort -u both orders and deduplicates in one pass, which is cheaper than piping into a separate uniq. -u compares the whole line here because no key was given.

instruction: Find entries present in the first sorted list but missing from the second.
context: comm prints three columns: lines only in file one, only in file two, and in both. Digits suppress columns, so -23 hides columns two and three and leaves only the first file's exclusives. Both inputs must already be sorted.

instruction: Find the entries that appear in both sorted lists.
context: comm: -12 suppresses the two exclusive columns and leaves the shared lines, which is the set intersection. Forgetting to sort the inputs produces silently wrong results rather than an error.

instruction: Merge two single-column files into one two-column table.
context: paste joins corresponding lines of its inputs side by side, and -d sets the delimiter between them. It pairs by position, so mismatched line counts leave trailing empty fields rather than an error.

instruction: Turn a space-aligned report into single-space-separated fields.
context: tr: -s squeezes repeated occurrences of the character into one. tr reads only from stdin and never takes a filename argument, which is why the redirect is required.

instruction: Find the twenty most common words in a document, ignoring case.
response: tr -cs '[:alpha:]' '\n' < book.txt | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20
context: tr: -c complements the set so everything that is not a letter becomes a separator, and -s collapses runs so blank lines do not appear. The second tr lowercases before counting so 'The' and 'the' merge.

instruction: Pull just the version number out of lines that look like 'version = 1.2.3'.
context: sed: -n suppresses the automatic print so only the explicit p flag emits, turning substitute into an extractor. -E enables extended regex so the capture group needs no backslashes, and \1 references it.

instruction: Strip an HTML comment block spanning several lines from a file.
context: sed: two addresses separated by a comma form a range that starts at the first match and ends at the next match of the second, inclusive. d deletes every line in that range.

instruction: Print only lines 100 through 120 of a large file.
context: sed: a numeric range address selects lines by number, and -n with p prints only those. Adding '120q' after would also stop reading the file early, which matters for very large inputs.

instruction: Compare the sorted contents of two directories without creating temporary files.
context: Process substitution: <(...) runs a command and presents its output as a filename backed by a file descriptor, so tools that require file arguments can read a pipeline. This avoids the mktemp-and-clean-up dance entirely.

instruction: Find which installed packages are missing from a requirements list.
context: Process substitution supplies comm with the two sorted inputs it demands without temporary files. -13 keeps only the lines exclusive to the second input, which are the packages installed but unlisted.

instruction: Send build output to a log while also filtering errors to the terminal in real time.
context: Process substitution: >(...) is the output direction, giving tee a writable filename that feeds another pipeline. This fans one stream into several independent consumers without reading the input twice.

instruction: Count how many distinct users triggered an authentication failure.
response: grep 'authentication failure' auth.log | grep -oE 'user=[a-z]+' | sort -u | wc -l
context: grep: -o prints only the matched portion rather than the whole line, which turns grep into a field extractor. -E enables the extended syntax needed for the character class and quantifier.

instruction: Skip the header row of a CSV and show the first five data rows.
context: tail: -n +2 starts output at line two rather than showing the last two lines, which is what a plain -n 2 would do. The plus sign is what flips it from 'last N' to 'from line N onward'.

instruction: Sort a tab-separated report numerically by its third column.
context: sort: -t sets the field delimiter, where $'\t' is ANSI-C quoting for a literal tab. -k3,3n confines the key to column three and applies numeric comparison to that key alone rather than the whole line.

instruction: Sort a report by department alphabetically, then by salary descending within each department.
context: sort: multiple -k options apply in order, so ties on the first key are broken by the second. Modifiers such as n and r attach to their own key rather than the whole command, which is why 3,3nr is written that way.

instruction: Convert an array of JSON objects into a CSV file with a header row.
context: jq: keys_unsorted preserves the original field order, binding it to $k for reuse. @csv quotes and escapes each row correctly, and -r stops jq from adding a second layer of JSON quoting around the result.

instruction: Fetch a JSON API and list the names of the returned items.
context: The -f flag matters in a pipeline: without it curl writes an HTML error page to stdout on a 500 and jq fails with a confusing parse error instead of the real HTTP failure.

instruction: Show the ten processes using the most resident memory.
context: ps: -o selects output columns and --sort with a leading minus orders descending. rss is resident set size in kilobytes. head -11 accounts for the header line consuming one of the rows.

instruction: Count how many commits each author has made, ranked.
context: git log: --format='%aN' prints the author name with .mailmap applied, which merges the same person's multiple email addresses. The rest is the standard count-and-rank pipeline.

instruction: Identify files with identical contents anywhere in this tree.
response: find . -type f -print0 | xargs -0 -r sha256sum | sort | uniq -w64 -d
context: uniq: -w limits the comparison to the first N characters, and a SHA-256 hex digest is exactly 64, so only the hash participates while the filename rides along. -d then shows only the groups that repeat.

instruction: Render a comma-separated file as an aligned table for reading.
context: column: -t builds a table by aligning columns to their widest cell, and -s sets the input separator. Without -t the input is merely filled into columns rather than aligned by field.

instruction: Re-run a status check every two seconds and highlight what changes.
context: watch: -n sets the interval in seconds and -d highlights cells that differ from the previous run. The command must be quoted so watch receives it as one argument rather than having the shell split it.

instruction: Check the uptime of every host listed in a file, four at a time.
context: xargs: -a reads the argument list from a file instead of stdin. BatchMode=yes makes ssh fail immediately rather than blocking on a password prompt, which is essential when running unattended in parallel.

instruction: Show each stack trace with the five lines that led up to it.
context: grep: -B N prints N lines before each match and -A N prints them after. Piping into less keeps the pager available for long results, since grep itself does no paging.

instruction: Search rotated gzip log files for an error without decompressing them to disk.
context: zgrep decompresses on the fly and passes the stream to grep. -h suppresses the filename prefix that grep adds automatically when given more than one file, keeping the output uniform.

instruction: Break a huge dataset into chunks of one million lines each.
context: split: -l splits on line count, -d uses numeric rather than alphabetic suffixes, and --additional-suffix preserves the extension so downstream tools still recognise the format. The final argument is the output prefix.

instruction: Number every line of a file including the blank ones.
context: nl: -b sets the body numbering style, where a numbers all lines and t, the default, numbers only non-empty ones. This difference is why nl and cat -n disagree on files containing blank lines.

instruction: Compress a file while keeping the original in place.
context: gzip: -k keeps the input file, which gzip otherwise deletes on success, and -c writes to stdout. -9 selects maximum compression at the cost of speed; -1 is the fast end of the range.

instruction: Look for an embedded version string inside a compiled binary.
context: strings extracts printable sequences from binary data, and -n sets the minimum run length to filter out short accidental matches. Piping to grep narrows the still-large result set.

instruction: Watch a log live but show only the lines mentioning errors.
context: tail: capital -F keeps following across log rotation by reopening the path, whereas lowercase -f holds the original inode and goes silent after a rotate. grep --line-buffered flushes each matching line immediately instead of buffering in 4 KiB blocks.

instruction: Sort a file and write the result back to the same file safely.
context: sort: -o names the output file and sort explicitly supports it being the same as an input, reading fully before writing. The naive 'sort f > f' truncates the file to zero bytes before sort ever reads it.

instruction: Find the ten busiest client IPs in an access log on macOS.
response: awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10
context: awk, sort, uniq, and head are all POSIX-specified for this usage, so the count-and-rank pipeline is identical on macOS. Only GNU-specific extensions such as sort -h would need changing.

instruction: Compare two sorted directory listings on macOS without temporary files.
context: Process substitution is a shell feature, and macOS defaults to Zsh, so <(...) works without change. It is unavailable only under a strict POSIX sh such as dash.

instruction: Copy a directory tree to a remote host through ssh without a temporary archive.
context: tar: a bare - as the -f argument means stdout when creating and stdin when extracting, which is what lets the archive stream through the pipe. -C sets the destination directory on the receiving side.

instruction: Force a program to flush its output line by line when piped.
context: stdbuf: -oL sets stdout to line buffering, overriding the full buffering libc selects automatically when stdout is a pipe rather than a terminal. This is why output seems to stall until a program exits.

instruction: Pretty-print a small JSON string held in a shell variable.
context: Here-strings: <<< feeds a single string to stdin without a pipe or temporary file. The variable must be quoted so its internal whitespace and newlines are preserved rather than word-split.

instruction: Capture only the warnings and errors from a build, discarding normal output.
context: Redirection is applied left to right: 2> sends stderr to the file, then > discards stdout. Reversing the order would point stderr at the terminal because 2>&1 semantics depend on what stdout referred to at that moment.

instruction: Run a reachability probe silently and rely only on its exit status.
context: The order matters: > /dev/null repoints stdout first, then 2>&1 makes stderr follow it to the same place. Writing 2>&1 first would duplicate the terminal, leaving stderr visible. ping -c limits the probe count and -W bounds the wait in seconds.
